title: Pleuritic chest pain on day 5 after hip fracture surgery
desc: This station involves a focused chest pain history and examination of a 47-year-old builder on the orthopaedic ward, day 5 after surgery for a right neck of femur fracture. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations, ECG, bloods and CT pulmonary angiogram, starts management of a haemodynamically stable pulmonary embolism, explains it to him and safety-nets.
focus: Postoperative pleuritic chest pain: a systems-based chest pain history, then recognising and managing pulmonary embolism
stem: You are the surgical resident on the orthopaedic ward of a busy metropolitan hospital. Chong Loh is a 47-year-old builder who had an operation for a right neck of femur fracture five days ago. His nurse has asked you to review him because he is complaining of chest pain.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Loh about his presenting complaint and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you his observations, his ECG, his blood results and the report of his CT pulmonary angiogram. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Chong Loh, a 47-year-old builder. You are sitting up in bed on the orthopaedic ward. You are anxious and a little short of breath, but you can speak in full sentences. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

What the nurse reports (the examiner says this if the candidate asks the nurse): "He called me a few minutes ago with chest pain. I did his obs at 14:40: heart rate 124, breathing 26, saturation 92% on room air, blood pressure 132/84 and temperature 37.8. This morning everything was normal. I gave him his paracetamol and helped him change position, but neither helped."

Opening line: "Doctor, I have chest pain!"

The pain (give only when asked):

  • Site: point to the right lower side of your chest, towards the back. It does not go to your neck, jaw, arms or back.
  • Onset: it came on quite quickly, about 30 minutes ago, while you were lying in bed.
  • Character: "It feels like a sharp pain." It is not crushing, heavy or tearing.
  • Severity: 5 out of 10.
  • Worse: taking a deep breath.
  • Better: nothing. Paracetamol did not help and changing position did not help. Leaning forward makes no difference.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • Breathlessness: you have felt short of breath for about 2 hours, since before the pain started.
  • Right calf: since early this morning, about 2 or 3 am (about 12 hours ago), your right calf has been sore, swollen and red. You thought it was from the operation. The left leg is fine.
  • No cough, no coughing up blood, no fainting or feeling faint, no palpitations.
  • No sweating, nausea or vomiting.
  • No fever or shivers that you have noticed. No phlegm.
  • No heartburn, sour taste, pain on swallowing or difficulty swallowing. No link to food. No tummy pain.
  • No breathlessness lying flat, no waking at night breathless, and no swelling of both legs.
  • No injury to the chest. You are not anxious by nature and have never had a panic attack.
  • No night sweats, weight loss or tiredness before the accident.

The accident and admission (only if asked): you fell from a height at work (from scaffolding) and broke your right hip. There were no other significant injuries; you did not hit your chest. The surgeons said the operation went well with no complications. You have not been getting out of bed much because it hurts; you have been up to the chair a couple of times with the physio.

Past medical history: appendix out at age 14. Nothing else. No previous clots in the legs or lungs, no heart or lung problems, no cancer. If asked your weight: 98 kg (BMI 31).

Medications: "I've been having regular Panadol and ibuprofen only when I need it for the pain. I've also been getting the injection in the tummy to thin the blood, I think they called it Clexane." You do not know the dose and do not think any were missed.

Allergies: none.

Family history: both parents alive, both have high blood pressure. Your father had an operation for bowel cancer this year and is recovering well. Your son is 17 and healthy. No one in the family has had blood clots, as far as you know.

Social history: you smoke 20 cigarettes a day and have since age 20. Alcohol is minimal: occasionally 1 or 2 beers at social events. You live in a suburban house with your wife and son. You eat a lot of fatty food and takeaway. Building work is physically demanding and you do no exercise outside work.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: "I've no idea why my chest would be hurting." You are worried: "Is this a heart attack?" You want to know what is going on and want the pain to stop.

Response to the candidate: if the candidate sits you up, reassures you and arranges oxygen, you feel a little less breathless, but the pain on breathing stays the same. If asked something outside the script, give a realistic answer.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: anxious, mildly short of breath at rest, speaking in full sentences. Not sweaty, not cyanosed, not pale. Alert.
  • Vital signs (14:40 set): HR 124 beats/min regular; BP 132/84 mmHg right arm, 130/82 mmHg left arm; RR 26/min; SpO2 92% on room air; temperature 37.8 °C.
  • Cardiovascular: pulse regular and equal in both radial arms. JVP not raised. Heart sounds dual with no murmur and no pericardial rub. Peripheral pulses present and equal.
  • Respiratory: trachea midline. Chest expansion equal. Percussion resonant throughout. Vesicular breath sounds throughout with no crackles, wheeze or pleural rub.
  • Chest wall: no tenderness over the sternum, costal cartilages or ribs, so the pain cannot be reproduced. No bruising or deformity.
  • Legs: the right calf is swollen, red and warm, and tender along the deep veins. Right calf circumference is 4 cm more than the left (measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity). Pitting oedema of the right ankle and shin. The left leg is normal.
  • Right hip wound: clean and dry with intact dressings; no redness, swelling or discharge.
  • Abdomen: soft and non-tender.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self by name and role (surgical resident), confirms the patient's identity and gains consent.
Acknowledges his pain and fear, stays calm and uses plain language throughout.
History
Characterises the chest pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: right lower chest, not radiating.
Onset, character and severity: sudden onset 30 minutes ago, sharp, 5/10.
Aggravating and relieving factors: worse on deep breathing (pleuritic), not relieved by paracetamol or changing position.

check.x: Asks about breathlessness and its timing (2 hours), and about other features of pulmonary embolism: cough, haemoptysis, fainting or near-fainting, palpitations.
Asks about leg symptoms and finds a painful, swollen, red right calf since early this morning (about 12 hours).
Screens for differentials across at least four systems:
check.d: Source marking: full marks for asking about differentials from at least 4 systems. Sub-items 1 and 2 together count as the cardiovascular system.

kids.x: Screens for ACS (crushing pain, radiation to neck/jaw/arm, sweating, nausea) and aortic dissection (tearing pain to the back).
Pericarditis (relief on leaning forward), heart failure (orthopnoea, PND, bilateral leg swelling).
Respiratory: sudden breathlessness or chest trauma (pneumothorax); fever and productive cough (pneumonia).
Gastrointestinal: burning pain, relation to food or lying flat (reflux), dysphagia (oesophageal spasm), epigastric pain with vomiting (pancreatitis).
Musculoskeletal or psychological: chest injury or localised tenderness (rib fracture, costochondritis); anxiety or panic attacks.

check.x: Clarifies the admission: mechanism of injury (fall from height), no other injuries including to the chest, no operative complications, and how little he has mobilised since surgery.
Asks about other risk factors for venous thromboembolism:

kids.x: Previous clots, known clotting disorder or family history of clots.
Symptoms of cancer (fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue).
Smoking with pack-years (about 27) and weight or BMI (98 kg, BMI 31).

check.x: Takes a medication history including enoxaparin thromboprophylaxis (dose and any missed doses) and as-needed ibuprofen, and asks about allergies (nil).
Covers past history (appendicectomy), family history (father's bowel cancer this year, no family VTE) and social history (alcohol, home, work).
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations, including his fear that this is a heart attack.
Examination
Requests a full set of vital signs and identifies tachycardia (124), tachypnoea (26), SpO2 92% on room air and low-grade fever with a normal blood pressure.
General inspection: distress, work of breathing, ability to speak in sentences, sweating, cyanosis, pallor.
Cardiovascular examination: pulse rate and rhythm, blood pressure in both arms, JVP, heart sounds and a pericardial rub.
Respiratory examination: tracheal position, expansion, percussion and auscultation for pneumothorax, consolidation, effusion or a pleural rub.
Palpates the chest wall for tenderness (none, so the pain is not musculoskeletal).
Examines and compares both legs: swelling with calf circumference measured, redness, warmth, tenderness along the deep veins and pitting oedema.
Inspects the right hip wound and briefly examines the abdomen.
Interpretation

Observations: RR, SpO2 and HR in the yellow zone, worse on the 15:10 room air set and only partly improved on 2 L/min oxygen (still yellow zone), BP normal; recognises he is haemodynamically stable but unwell, and that this needs clinical review, escalation and closer monitoring.
Calculates the Wells score (9: DVT signs, PE most likely, HR over 100, recent surgery) as PE likely, and states that a D-dimer is not needed and he should go straight to CTPA.
ECG: sinus tachycardia with no ST elevation or ischaemic change and no right heart strain; unchanged from the pre-operative ECG apart from the rate.

Bloods: two normal troponins (against ACS), Hb 118 (post-operative fall, a baseline before anticoagulation), normal platelets (no thrombocytopenia on enoxaparin), and normal creatinine and INR (safe for contrast and anticoagulation).
CTPA: acute bilateral lower lobe pulmonary emboli with no CT evidence of right heart strain (RV:LV 0.8).
Notes the small right lower lobe infarct with effusion as the cause of the right pleuritic pain and low-grade fever, and no pneumothorax, consolidation elsewhere or aortic abnormality.
Risk stratifies: haemodynamically stable so not high risk; HR 110 or more (sPESI 1) but normal right ventricle and troponin, so intermediate-low risk.
Management
Immediate care: ABCDE, sits him up, oxygen titrated to SpO2 92 to 96%, IV access and closer monitoring of observations.
Escalates to the orthopaedic registrar and consultant, and involves the medical registrar or haematology (thrombosis) team.

Starts therapeutic anticoagulation now (accept a statement that it should have been started while awaiting CTPA given the high probability, bleeding risk permitting), with the surgical team agreeing on the bleeding risk:

kids.x: Stops the prophylactic enoxaparin (no double dosing) and checks when the last dose was given.

Gives a correct regimen: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC 12-hourly (about 100 mg for 98 kg), or apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily, or rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily with food for 21 days then 20 mg daily with food.
Names unfractionated heparin by infusion as the option if bleeding risk is high or rapid reversal may be needed.

check.x: Thrombolysis not indicated (haemodynamically stable; surgery and trauma 5 days ago is a contraindication); if he becomes shocked, rapid response and urgent reperfusion decision with ICU.
check.d: Credit either 'absolute' (ESC) or 'relative' (AHA) as long as recent surgery or trauma is named as a contraindication.

check.x: Ongoing plan: 3 months anticoagulation (provoked PE) then review; mobilise with physio once anticoagulated; smoking cessation (NRT in hospital, Quitline).
Explains in plain words that this is not a heart attack (normal ECG and troponins) but a clot from his leg that has travelled to his lungs, treated with blood thinners, and checks his understanding.
Safety netting
Tells him to press the call bell straight away in hospital, or call 000 after discharge, for worsening breathlessness or chest pain, fainting or coughing up blood.

Explains the bleeding warning signs on blood thinners: black or bloody stools, blood in the urine, vomiting blood, bleeding from the wound, a severe headache. Advises avoiding anti-inflammatories and checking with a pharmacist before any new medicine.
Arranges follow-up: GP discharge summary and GP review within a week; review at 3 months.

part2.lead: Here are Mr Loh's observations, his ECG, his blood results and the report of his CT pulmonary angiogram.
part2.patient:
When the candidate explains, Mr Loh asks, if not already covered:

  • "So it's not my heart? I'm not having a heart attack?"
  • "Won't a blood thinner make my hip bleed?"
  • "How long will I need to be on it?"

He is relieved once he hears clearly that it is not a heart attack and that the clot can be treated.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Weight 98 kg. Room air at 14:40 and 15:10; on 2 L/min nasal prongs since 15:15 (went to CT on oxygen). The 08:00 set this morning was all in the white zone: HR 86, RR 16, SpO2 97%, BP 130/80, temperature 37.1 °C.
handover.model:
Read: on room air at 14:40 and 15:10, RR 26 then 28 (yellow zone), SpO2 92% then 91% (yellow zone), HR 124 then 126 (yellow zone). At 15:45 on 2 L/min nasal prongs: RR 26, SpO2 94% and HR 122, all still in the yellow zone. BP 132/84, 128/80 and 128/78 and temperature 37.7 to 37.8 °C are in the white zone, and he is alert. The 08:00 set was entirely normal.

For Mr Loh: an acute change with several yellow-zone values that got worse on room air and have only partly improved with oxygen: hypoxaemia, tachypnoea and tachycardia with a low-grade fever. His blood pressure is normal, so he is not shocked (not high-risk or massive PE).

What it changes: the yellow zone calls for a clinical review, which is why the resident has been called. With several values in the yellow zone, escalate early to the registrar. Continue oxygen titrated to SpO2 92 to 96% and observe him more often. Call a rapid response if any value reaches the red zone on his chart (SBP 90 mmHg or less, SpO2 90% or less, HR 140 or more, RR 30 or more, or a new drop in consciousness), or if staff are seriously worried or he deteriorates despite review.

rows.note: Chest pain reported; resident called for clinical review
Repeat set by nurse before oxygen applied; still breathless
Back from CTPA on 2 L/min nasal prongs; a little less breathless

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG at 14:50, recorded during chest pain.

  • Rate: 124 beats/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus tachycardia.
  • Axis: +60°.
  • PR interval: 150 ms.
  • QRS: 88 ms.
  • QT 300 ms, QTc 431 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation or depression in any territory. T waves upright in the inferior and lateral leads and in V2 to V6.
  • Other: no right bundle branch block, no S1Q3T3 pattern, no pathological Q waves, no right ventricular strain pattern.
  • Comparison: pre-operative ECG 5 days ago showed sinus rhythm at 78 beats/min and was otherwise identical; the only change is the rate.
handover.model:
Read: sinus tachycardia at 124 with a normal axis and intervals. No ST elevation or depression, no new T wave inversion, and no RBBB, S1Q3T3 or right ventricular strain. Compared with the pre-operative ECG, only the rate has changed.

For Mr Loh: no STEMI or ischaemic change during pain, which argues against ACS, his main fear. Sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding in PE. The absence of strain changes is consistent with a normal right ventricle.

What it changes: no ACS pathway or cath lab. It supports going ahead with CTPA, and the tracing is kept as a baseline.

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected on the ward at 14:50 (repeat troponin at 15:50). No haemolysis. D-dimer not requested.
handover.model:
Read: Hb 118 g/L, down from 146 before surgery: an expected post-operative fall with a normal white cell count. Platelets 298, higher than before surgery. Sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine 84 and eGFR above 90 are normal. LFTs are normal apart from albumin 33. INR 1.0 and APTT 31 are normal. hs-troponin T is 9 then 10 ng/L at 0 and 1 hour, below the 99th centile with no significant change.

For Mr Loh: the two normal troponins argue against myocardial infarction and show no myocardial injury from the PE. Normal renal function makes contrast for CTPA safe and allows full-dose enoxaparin or a DOAC. A normal platelet count on day 5 of enoxaparin makes heparin-induced thrombocytopenia unlikely.

What it changes: these are his baselines (Hb, platelets, creatinine, coagulation) before therapeutic anticoagulation. With a Wells score of 9 a D-dimer adds nothing, because it rules PE out only when probability is low.

labs.title: Urea, electrolytes and creatinine; liver function tests

handover.label: CT pulmonary angiogram report
handover.result:
Examination: CT pulmonary angiogram, performed 15:35. IV iodinated contrast given (pulmonary arterial phase).

Clinical details: 47-year-old man, day 5 after surgery for a right neck of femur fracture. Sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness, swollen right calf, HR 124, SpO2 92% on room air.

Comparison: none.

Findings:

  • Pulmonary arteries: good opacification. Filling defects in the right lower lobe pulmonary artery extending into the anterior, lateral and posterior basal segmental arteries, occlusive in the posterior basal branch. Non-occlusive filling defects in the left lower lobe lateral and posterior basal segmental arteries. The main, right and left pulmonary arteries are clear, with no saddle embolus. Main pulmonary artery 26 mm.
  • Heart: RV to LV diameter ratio 0.8. No flattening or bowing of the interventricular septum. No reflux of contrast into the IVC or hepatic veins. No pericardial effusion.
  • Lungs: a 25 mm pleural-based, wedge-shaped ground-glass and consolidative opacity in the posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe, in keeping with early pulmonary infarction or haemorrhage. No consolidation elsewhere. No pneumothorax.
  • Pleura: small right pleural effusion.
  • Mediastinum: thoracic aorta of normal calibre with no intimal flap seen, within the limits of a pulmonary arterial phase study. No lymphadenopathy.
  • Bones and upper abdomen: no rib fracture. Upper abdomen unremarkable.

Conclusion: acute bilateral lower lobe pulmonary emboli with no CT evidence of right heart strain. Small right lower lobe pulmonary infarct with a small right pleural effusion.
handover.model:
Read: acute bilateral PE. There are lobar and segmental filling defects in the right lower lobe and segmental defects in the left lower lobe. The main pulmonary arteries are clear, with no saddle embolus. The right ventricle is not dilated (RV:LV 0.8, below 1.0), with no septal bowing and no contrast reflux. A peripheral wedge-shaped opacity is a small pulmonary infarct with a small effusion. There is no pneumothorax, no pneumonia, no rib fracture and no aortic abnormality.

For Mr Loh: this confirms the diagnosis. The infarct irritating the pleura explains his right-sided pleuritic pain and low-grade fever. With a normal BP, a normal right ventricle and normal troponins, he is at intermediate-low risk (sPESI 1 because his HR is 110 or more). The PE is provoked by major orthopaedic surgery and immobility, with the right calf DVT the likely source.

What it changes: start therapeutic anticoagulation now (or continue it if already started while awaiting the scan). Thrombolysis is not indicated. A venous leg ultrasound is not needed to make the diagnosis.

ask: You are now calling the orthopaedic registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Mr Loh, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer, including how his pre-test probability guided the choice of investigation.
Outline your management of Mr Loh now, here on the orthopaedic ward.
Mr Loh asks you whether he has had a heart attack. What would you tell him, what warning signs would you give him, and what follow-up would you arrange for when he goes home?
expect:
• Identify: self, surgical resident on the orthopaedic ward. Chong Loh, 47, day 5 after surgery for a right neck of femur fracture.
  • Situation: sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness for 2 hours. CTPA confirms bilateral PE.
  • Background: right calf swollen and red since early this morning. Barely mobilising. On prophylactic enoxaparin. Smokes 20 a day. BMI 31. No previous VTE.
  • Assessment: HR 126, RR 28, SpO2 91% RA (yellow), now 94% on 2 L; BP normal. ECG sinus tachycardia only, troponins normal x2. CTPA bilateral lower lobe PE, no RV strain, small right lower lobe infarct explaining the pleuritic pain. Intermediate-low risk.
  • Recommendation: agree to start therapeutic anticoagulation now. Oxygen and closer monitoring. Please review within the hour. Rapid response if he becomes hypotensive.

Most likely: acute bilateral pulmonary embolism from a right calf DVT, provoked by surgery and immobility. For it: day 5 after major orthopaedic surgery, poor mobility, sudden right-sided pleuritic pain, breathlessness, tachycardia, hypoxaemia, a swollen right calf, smoker, BMI 31. CTPA confirms it.

Wells 9 (DVT signs 3, PE most likely 3, HR >100 1.5, surgery within 4 weeks 1.5): PE likely, so a D-dimer is not needed (after surgery it would be raised anyway) and he went straight to CTPA.

  • ACS: he fears it and is a smoker with a poor diet. Against it: sharp pleuritic pain, no ischaemic ECG change, two normal troponins.
  • Aortic dissection: against it: no tearing pain to the back, equal arm BPs, normal aorta on CT.
  • Hospital-acquired pneumonia: pleuritic pain and low-grade fever after surgery. Against it: no productive cough, a clear chest, no consolidation.
  • Pericarditis or pneumothorax: against it: no positional relief, no rub, a normal ECG, and no pneumothorax on CT.

1. Immediate: ABCDE. Sit him up. Oxygen to SpO2 92 to 96%. IV access. Closer observations.
  2. Escalate: orthopaedic registrar and consultant to agree on the bleeding risk. Involve the medical registrar or haematology.
  3. Anticoagulate now (accept a statement that it should have been started while awaiting CTPA given the high probability, bleeding risk permitting): baselines Hb 118 (pre-op 146), platelets, creatinine and INR normal. Stop prophylactic enoxaparin. One of: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC 12-hourly (about 100 mg), or apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily, or rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily with food for 21 days then 20 mg daily with food. UFH infusion if bleeding risk is high.
  4. No thrombolysis: not indicated (haemodynamically stable; surgery and trauma 5 days ago is a contraindication); if he becomes shocked, rapid response and urgent reperfusion decision with ICU.
  5. Regular paracetamol. Stop ibuprofen.
  6. Ongoing: 3 months (provoked) then review; physio mobilisation once anticoagulated; NRT and Quitline.

• In plain words: not a heart attack. The heart tracing and blood tests are normal. A clot from his leg has travelled to his lungs. Blood thinners stop it growing while his body clears it. The surgical team has checked that it is safe for his hip.
  • Red flags: in hospital, press the call bell. After discharge, call 000 for worse breathlessness or chest pain, fainting or coughing up blood.
  • Bleeding: watch for black or bloody stools, blood in the urine, vomiting blood, a bleeding wound or a severe headache, and see a doctor that day. Avoid anti-inflammatories. Check new medicines with the pharmacist.
  • Follow-up: GP discharge summary and GP review within a week; review at 3 months.

ddx.dx: Acute pulmonary embolism from a right calf deep vein thrombosis
ddx.for: Day 5 after major orthopaedic surgery with little mobilisation, sudden pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, HR 124, SpO2 92%, a swollen red right calf, Wells 9, and bilateral lower lobe emboli on CTPA.
ddx.against: He has been receiving prophylactic enoxaparin.

ddx.for: Chest pain in a 47-year-old male smoker (27 pack-years) with obesity and a high-fat diet.
ddx.against: Sharp right-sided pleuritic pain without radiation, sweating or nausea, no ischaemic change on the ECG, and two normal troponins.
Pain is not tearing and does not go to the back, BP is equal in both arms, and the aorta is normal on CT.

ddx.for: Pleuritic pain, breathlessness and a temperature of 37.8 °C after surgery while lying in bed.
ddx.against: No cough or sputum, a clear chest on examination and no consolidation on CT.

ddx.for: Sharp chest pain that is worse on breathing.
ddx.against: Right-sided rather than central, not relieved by leaning forward, no rub, no ST or PR changes on the ECG and no pericardial effusion.

ddx.for: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after a fall from height.
ddx.against: No chest injury, trachea midline, resonant chest with equal breath sounds, and no pneumothorax on CT.

guide:
Part 1 is set at about 14:45; ECG and bloods are taken at 14:50 during the review. In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. If the candidate asks the nurse, give the nurse's report. Credit differentials explored in the history in item 8: full credit needs questions from at least four systems. In Part 2 hand over all four results together and ask the four questions in order. Part 2 is set at about 16:00, after the CTPA (15:35) and the 1-hour troponin (15:50). Mr Loh puts his questions during the explanation if the candidate has not covered them. Credit item 24 if the Wells score and the reason for skipping a D-dimer are given in the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer. In item 33 accept recent surgery or trauma called either an absolute or a relative contraindication to thrombolysis.

A high-performing candidate characterises the pleuritic pain, picks up the 2 hours of breathlessness and the right calf symptoms, screens the cardiac, respiratory, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal and psychological causes, and examines both legs. In Part 2 they calculate a high Wells score and say a D-dimer is not needed. They read a normal ECG and troponins as against ACS, and recognise bilateral PE without right heart strain in a haemodynamically stable patient. They start oxygen to target, stop the prophylactic enoxaparin and start a correctly dosed therapeutic anticoagulant, agreeing the bleeding risk with the orthopaedic team. They state that thrombolysis is not indicated, and reassure him clearly that this is not a heart attack, with specific red flags and follow-up.

A borderline candidate takes a cardiac-only history, misses the calf, or orders a D-dimer despite high probability. They may add therapeutic anticoagulation on top of the prophylactic dose, keep the ibuprofen, suggest thrombolysis for a stable patient 5 days after surgery, or end with "come back if you are worried".
explain:
Diagnosis: provoked pulmonary embolism

Pulmonary embolism is obstruction of one or more pulmonary arteries, most often by thrombus from a deep vein thrombosis in the legs or pelvis. Mr Loh has the classic setting: major orthopaedic surgery 5 days ago after a fall from height, poor mobilisation, obesity (BMI 31) and heavy smoking. He also has a right calf that has been painful, swollen and red for 12 hours. Breathlessness is the most common symptom, followed by chest pain, which is usually pleuritic but not always. Haemoptysis is uncommon. Signs include tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypoxaemia and a low-grade fever, with shock in severe cases. Always look for a DVT. Thromboprophylaxis lowers the risk but does not remove it, so PE can occur on prophylactic enoxaparin.

A systems-based chest pain history

Chest pain needs a history that screens each system for the dangerous and common causes:

  • Cardiovascular: ACS (crushing pain, radiation, sweating, nausea), aortic dissection (tearing pain to the back, syncope), pericarditis (pleuritic pain relieved by leaning forward), arrhythmia (palpitations) and heart failure (orthopnoea, nocturnal breathlessness, leg oedema).
  • Respiratory: PE, pneumothorax (sudden pleuritic pain, trauma) and pneumonia (fever, productive cough).
  • Gastrointestinal: reflux, oesophageal spasm (dysphagia) and pancreatitis (epigastric pain, vomiting, alcohol, gallstones).
  • Musculoskeletal: rib fracture and costochondritis (pain reproduced on palpation).
  • Psychological: panic attack, a diagnosis of exclusion.

Mr Loh's pain is sharp and pleuritic with no positional relief, no reproducible tenderness and no features of ACS or dissection. His breathlessness began before the pain.

Pre-test probability and the choice of test

The Wells score sets the pre-test probability. Points: clinical signs of DVT 3, PE the most likely diagnosis 3, HR over 100 1.5, immobilisation or surgery in the past 4 weeks 1.5, previous PE or DVT 1.5, haemoptysis 1, active cancer 1. Mr Loh scores 9, so PE is likely. In low to moderate probability, a negative D-dimer can exclude PE, and a positive one leads to CTPA. In high probability a D-dimer is not needed: go straight to CTPA. D-dimer rules out; it does not rule in, and after surgery it will be raised anyway. A V/Q scan is the alternative when contrast is unsuitable (contrast allergy, severe renal impairment, pregnancy). A venous leg ultrasound confirms a DVT and is useful when CTPA is not possible. Here it is not needed for the diagnosis.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: RR, SpO2 and HR in the yellow zone, worse on room air and still in the yellow zone on 2 L/min oxygen, with a normal BP. On the local track-and-trigger chart (e.g. NSW Between the Flags) this needs a clinical review and escalation, with a rapid response call if any value reaches the red zone or staff are seriously worried.
  • ECG: done mainly to look for ACS. In PE it may show sinus tachycardia (the most common finding) or right heart strain (right axis, RBBB, T wave inversion in V1 to V4, S1Q3T3). His shows only sinus tachycardia.
  • Bloods: FBC, UEC, LFT and coagulation studies set the baseline for anticoagulation and look for infection or electrolyte problems. Normal renal function allows contrast, LMWH or a DOAC. Normal platelets on enoxaparin argue against heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Two normal troponins argue against myocardial infarction and show no myocardial injury.
  • CTPA: bilateral lower lobe emboli, a normal right ventricle and a small right lower lobe infarct, which explains the right-sided pleuritic pain.

Risk stratification

Management depends first on haemodynamic stability. High-risk (massive) PE means shock or sustained hypotension and calls for reperfusion. A stable patient is stratified further using clinical scores (sPESI), right ventricular size on CT or echo, and troponin. Mr Loh is stable with a normal right ventricle and troponin, but his HR is 110 or more, so he is intermediate-low risk. He stays an inpatient with closer monitoring.

Management (eTG)

  • Oxygen to a target SpO2 of 92 to 96% (TSANZ), analgesia with paracetamol, and stopping NSAIDs once he is anticoagulated.
  • With a high clinical probability, start therapeutic anticoagulation while awaiting CTPA unless bleeding risk is prohibitive (shortly after surgery, agree this with the surgical team); continue it once PE is confirmed, replacing the prophylactic dose. Options: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC 12-hourly, apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily, or rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily with food for 21 days then 20 mg daily with food. Unfractionated heparin by infusion is the option when bleeding risk is high or rapid reversal may be needed.
  • Thrombolysis is reserved for haemodynamically unstable PE. It is not indicated for Mr Loh because he is haemodynamically stable; major surgery and trauma within the past 3 weeks is a contraindication (absolute in ESC, relative in AHA) – if he became shocked, he would need a rapid response call, and reperfusion options (systemic, catheter-directed or surgical) would be decided urgently with ICU and the surgical team.
  • Duration: a PE provoked by a major transient risk factor such as surgery is treated for 3 months, then reviewed.
  • Mobilise once he is anticoagulated, and support him to stop smoking.

Safety netting

Explain clearly that this is not a heart attack. Teach him the warning signs of a new or larger clot (worse breathlessness, chest pain, fainting, coughing up blood) and of bleeding on anticoagulants (black or bloody stools, blood in the urine, vomiting blood, a bleeding wound, a severe headache). Before discharge give anticoagulant education and a written plan, and send a discharge summary to the GP. Arrange GP review soon after discharge and a review at 3 months to decide on stopping anticoagulation.
points: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after major orthopaedic surgery is PE until proven otherwise: always examine both legs for a DVT.
A chest pain history screens every system (cardiac, respiratory, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, psychological) for the dangerous and common causes.
With a high Wells score (PE likely) go straight to CTPA: a D-dimer only rules PE out when the pre-test probability is low or moderate.

Haemodynamic stability drives management: stable PE gets therapeutic anticoagulation; thrombolysis is reserved for shock, and major surgery or trauma within the past 3 weeks is a contraindication (absolute in ESC, relative in AHA).
Replace the prophylactic enoxaparin with a therapeutic dose (do not double up), stop NSAIDs, agree the bleeding risk with the surgical team, and treat a surgically provoked PE for 3 months.
An ECG and troponin are mainly for excluding ACS; sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding in PE.
